title: Llama-modchip: 284B DeepSeek on 64GB RAM, no GPU
content:
TL;DR — The 3 Paradigm-Breaking Pillars of llama-modchip:
- 🐋 284.33B Frontier MoE in a 64 GB CPU Box: Shrinks DeepSeek-V4-Flash from 76.87 GiB (which crashes in OOM on 64 GB Linux) down to 56.56 GiB on disk / 57.61–58.9 GiB VmRSS at full 256K context (44.36 tok/s prefill, 9.06–10.74 tok/s pure CPU decode, 11.5–14.7 tok/s with PVS) using closed-form Analytical SwiGLU-H2 Second-Order Hessian Compression + Fractal-64 (Q2_0, 3.75 bpw) MLA transcoding + 4-Level Register (ZMM AVX-512BW) + L1D (32 KB) + L2 (1 MB) + L3 (64 MB) Whole-Model Tiling + $L_2$-Quadrature MoE Pruning.
- ⚡ 30B MoE at GPU Speeds on Pure CPU: Runs NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B in 14.35 GiB at 25.0–60.4 tok/s on 16-core Zen 5 (111.6 tok/s on Threadripper, 80.8 tok/s on AMD Vulkan Hybrid, 44.97 tok/s on AWS Graviton3 ARM64) via a 1.64 MB Stockfish-PVS v2 + RouteCrack L2/L3 Drafter (96.4% acceptance) and _MM_HINT_NTA L3 cache isolation (HARPCache).
- 🤖 Zero-API Claude Code (./modchip claude): Eliminates the 45-second CPU agent prompt re-evaluation bottleneck via /dev/shm Slot-0 KV Warm Restore (18.9 ms on Nemotron-30B / 13.1–32.6 ms on DeepSeek-284B) with all 40 Claude Code tools active.
🐧 Linux & 🍎 macOS (1-Command Automated Setup & Chat)
git clone https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip.git
cd llama-modchip
./modchip chat
⚡ Zero-Compile Direct Run (Pre-Compiled Linux x86_64 Binary + Hugging Face .gguf)
⚠️ Important Compatibility Note (GGML_TYPE_Q2_0 = 40): Our Fractal-64 models use custom block-64 BF16-scale Gray-coded tensors (GGML_TYPE_Q2_0, type ID 40) and custom deepseek4 / Stockfish-PVS kernels. Opening them in unpatched llama.cpp, Ollama, or LM Studio will fail with unknown tensor type 40. Use either ./modchip above or our standalone single-file pre-compiled binary (llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64, zero .so dependencies) bundled directly inside the Hugging Face repositories and GitHub Release v2.4.0:
# 1. For 30B Nemotron-3.5-A3B (14.35 GiB — runs in 16–32 GB RAM at 25–60.4 tok/s):
hf download Synchopate/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64-CPU-GGUF \
  llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64.gguf --local-dir .
chmod +x llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64
./llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 -m NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64.gguf -c 262144 -t 16 --port 8080
# 2. For 284B DeepSeek-V4-Flash (56.56 GiB — fits in 64 GB RAM at 9.1–14.7 tok/s):
hf download Synchopate/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Fractal-64GB-CPU-GGUF --local-dir ./dsv4
chmod +x ./dsv4/llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64
./dsv4/llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 -m ./dsv4/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Fractal-00001-of-00003.gguf -c 32768 -t 16 -fa on --port 8080
🪟 Windows 10/11 (1-Click Hybrid GPU + CPU MoE Pack)
Open windows/ and double-click windows/AVVIA_MODCHIP.bat (or run ./modchip start in Git Bash). It automatically detects your CPU cores, free RAM, and GPU VRAM (nvidia-smi), downloads official llama.cpp CUDA 12.4 / Vulkan binaries, computes the optimal --n-cpu-moe split, and opens the Web Chat UI (http://127.0.0.1:8080).
🏆 Can your CPU run a 284B Frontier MoE in 64 GB RAM? Test in 2 seconds (Zero Downloads):
curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/main/scripts/check_cpu_readiness.py | python3

report.summary: A GitHub project claims to run a 284B DeepSeek MoE at 256K context on a 64GB CPU-only box using custom 2-bit quantization, cache tiling and speculative decoding.
report.background: Local LLM inference has shifted from hobbyist curiosity to a real workload, driven by llama.cpp's GGUF format and a familiar quantization ladder (Q8 down to Q2) that trades fidelity for memory. Mixture-of-Experts models complicate this: a 284B-parameter model may activate only ~13B per token, so weights dominate memory while compute stays modest — exactly the profile that suits a CPU with lots of cheap DDR5. Meanwhile 64GB mini-PCs and Ryzen/Threadripper workstations have become common, and the gap between them and $30,000 multi-GPU rigs is a tempting target. llama-modchip sits in a wave of aggressive 'compression plus hand-tuned kernel' repositories that mix genuine engineering (AVX-512 tiling, speculative drafting, KV-cache reuse) with marketing-heavy claims. Its headline numbers are self-reported and, so far, not independently reproduced, so treat them as claims rather than established benchmarks.
key_points: DeepSeek-V4-Flash shrinks from 76.87 GiB (which OOMs on 64GB Linux) to ~56.5 GiB on disk at roughly 3.75 bits per weight. Reported throughput is about 44 tok/s prefill and 9–14.7 tok/s decode on a 16-core Zen 5 laptop chip with no GPU — usable for batch jobs, painful for interactive chat.

The 30B Nemotron-A3B model is the more practical story: 14.35 GiB and 25–60 tok/s on the same CPU, achieved with a 1.64MB speculative drafter claiming 96.4% acceptance plus L3 cache-isolation hints. That puts a competent mid-size MoE at roughly conversational speed on commodity hardware.

Compatibility is deliberately broken. Models use a custom tensor type (GGML_TYPE_Q2_0, ID 40) and custom kernels, so stock llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio will fail with 'unknown tensor type 40'. You must use the project's own binaries — convenient, but it fragments the ecosystem and complicates trust.

The repo also targets coding agents: './modchip claude' keeps a KV cache warm in /dev/shm so Claude Code's 40 tools resume in 19–33ms instead of re-evaluating a long prompt for ~45 seconds — a real bottleneck for CPU-bound agentic loops.

Distribution is aggressively productized: one-command Linux/macOS setup, a Windows hybrid GPU+CPU batch file that auto-computes MoE offload splits, and a zero-download readiness checker feeding a community leaderboard. That invites outside verification, which the project still needs.
report.impact: If the numbers hold up, the economics of frontier-class inference shift: a $1,500–3,000 64GB DDR5 mini-PC becomes a plausible host for air-gapped code intelligence, security auditing and agent fleets that previously demanded a multi-GPU server. For developers, it is a reminder that CPU-side work — AVX-512 kernels, L1/L2/L3 tiling, speculative decoding, KV reuse — still yields large multiples, and that the llama.cpp fork ecosystem is where a lot of that experimentation now happens. For regular users, the realistic gain is privacy and zero API cost, not speed: 9 tokens per second is fine for reports, not for live chat. The caveats matter more than the headline — 2-bit quantization can quietly degrade reasoning, the 100/100 'quality gate' is self-graded, and custom forks invite lock-in and supply-chain scrutiny. Independent reproduction is the deciding variable.
report.tools: To follow up, watch llama.cpp and the performance-oriented fork ik_llama.cpp for the kernels this project borrows from; KTransformers for MoE CPU/GPU offload ideas; Ollama and LM Studio for the user-friendly baseline these models won't load into. Validate any 2-bit claim yourself with lm-eval-harness or the repo's own eval script before trusting it. The project's check_cpu_readiness.py gives a quick yes/no on your hardware, and llamafile is worth knowing for single-file distribution patterns.
